rationale: These are raw recordings with no artifact rejection, so a few eye-blink, movement or electrode-pop segments can dominate a mean-averaged Welch spectrum, especially in the low (delta/theta) bands where schizophrenia effects are reported. I'm switching Welch's segment averaging from mean to median. Median averaging is a well-established artifact-robust estimator, so the band powers should reflect each subject's typical background EEG rather than rare bursts. That should also make them more stable on the shorter 1-minute external recordings.

Schizophrenia EEG typically shows a slower alpha (more power in 8–10 Hz relative to 10–13 Hz) and changes in beta that differ between low and high beta. The 8–13 Hz and 13–30 Hz bands are too wide to capture this, so I split them into alpha1/alpha2 and beta1/beta2. The features stay as log relative power, so they remain unaffected by amplitude scale for the external sets. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm making one preprocessing change: switch every recording to the average reference and use median-averaged Welch PSDs. The data has no artifact rejection and its reference is unknown, and the external MSU/RepOD clinics probably use different references. Median averaging limits the effect of short artifacts such as blinks and movement bursts in the 5-minute recordings. The average reference makes relative band-power topographies more comparable across sites, so the schizophrenia slow-wave and alpha differences should be easier to separate from recording setup. I haven't run this; the harness will give its Dev score.

I'm switching Welch's PSD from the default mean across segments to a median across segments. The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blinks, muscle bursts or electrode pops can dominate the mean spectrum. The median gives a robust per-subject spectrum, which should reduce noise in the relative band-power features on the dev set and on the external clinics/amplifiers.

I'm adding one per-channel feature: the aperiodic (1/f) exponent, fitted to the log-log PSD over 2–40 Hz with the alpha range (7–14 Hz) left out. Schizophrenia has been linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up as a change in this exponent and is something relative band power can't capture. The exponent also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so it should carry over to external amplifiers.

These recordings have no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD can be skewed by a few windows with blinks, movement or muscle bursts. This change switches Welch to median averaging across segments, which makes each subject's spectrum (and its relative band powers) robust to these transient artifacts. It should also travel better to the external clinics' data.

I'm adding one feature per channel: the aperiodic (1/f) slope of the Welch PSD, fit in log-log space from 2–40 Hz with 7–14 Hz excluded so the alpha peak doesn't distort it. Schizophrenia has been linked to a shifted excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up in the 1/f exponent. Relative band power partly mixes this up with oscillatory power. Unlike absolute power, the slope doesn't change with amplitude scale, which matters for the external datasets.

These recordings have no artifact cleaning, so a few seconds of eye movement or muscle activity can dominate the mean Welch PSD. That would inflate delta and gamma and swamp the real schizophrenia differences (more slow-wave activity, less alpha). Taking the median across Welch segments instead of the mean makes the band powers robust to these bursts without changing anything else. It should also hold up better on the external sets, where artifact rates and recording lengths differ.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few large-artifact segments (eye movements, muscle bursts, electrode pops) can skew the usual mean-averaged Welch PSD. Switching Welch to median averaging over the 2-s segments gives robust per-channel spectra. This should sharpen the slowing and alpha differences between schizophrenia and controls, and make the features more stable on short, noisier external recordings (MSU has only 1 min).

Two well-replicated schizophrenia findings are slower alpha (power shifts from upper to lower alpha) and more theta. The 5 broad bands average over both shifts, so I'm splitting theta (4–6 / 6–8 Hz), alpha (8–10 / 10–13 Hz) and beta (13–20 / 20–30 Hz). Each feature is still a log ratio of band power to total power, so the model stays robust to amplitude scale and recording length on the external sets.

I'm adding a second branch that captures how channels co-vary, alongside the existing spectral branch, and averaging the two models' predicted probabilities. Schizophrenia involves altered functional connectivity, which relative band power can't see. In the new branch the signal is re-referenced to the average, then for each of delta, theta, alpha and beta I estimate per-epoch covariances, take their Riemannian mean and scale it by its trace, and map it to tangent space (fitted on the training fold only). Trace scaling makes the features insensitive to amplitude scale, and the average reference makes them less dependent on the original reference. Both matter for the external datasets.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so blinks, movement and muscle bursts in a few Welch segments inflate the mean PSD. This hits delta and beta/gamma relative power hardest, and those are the bands where the schizophrenia slowing and gamma effects live. Averaging the Welch segments by median instead of mean (with 50% overlap) is a robust spectral estimate that should reduce that subject-level noise and transfer better to the external clinics' recordings.

I'm adding one aperiodic (1/f) exponent per channel to the current log relative band powers. It is the log-log PSD slope over 2–40 Hz, fitted with the alpha peak (7–14 Hz) left out. Schizophrenia is linked to altered excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up as a flatter or steeper 1/f slope. The slope also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so it should carry over to the external amplifiers.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few movement or muscle bursts can dominate a mean-averaged Welch spectrum. Different clinics also use different references. I'll re-reference to the common average and take the median across 4-s Welch segments instead of the mean, which should make the log relative band powers less sensitive to artifacts and to reference choice. That should help the dev score and the transfer to the external MSU and RepOD sets.

Re-reference every recording to the common average, and average the Welch segments with a median instead of a mean. The aim is relative band-power topographies that don't depend on the original reference (which differs between ASEEG, MSU and RepOD) and that ignore short high-amplitude artifacts such as blinks, movement and electrode pops in this unprocessed data. Relative power already cancels amplitude scale, so this covers the other two robustness problems the brief raises.

I'm adding a second, complementary view: tangent-space features from each subject's covariance matrix over 1–45 Hz. Each matrix is shrinkage-estimated and trace-normalized, so it is independent of amplitude scale. Schizophrenia is linked to disturbed large-scale coupling between channels, which per-channel relative power cannot capture. I train a separate regularized logistic regression on this view and average its probabilities with the existing band-power model. The Riemannian reference mean is fitted on the training fold only.

Two well-replicated schizophrenia EEG markers aren't captured by fixed relative band powers: a slower individual alpha peak frequency and a changed aperiodic (1/f) exponent. This change adds a per-channel aperiodic slope (fitted in log-log space over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha range) and a posterior alpha centre-of-gravity frequency. Both are unaffected by amplitude scale, which should help on the external sets.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few high-amplitude segments (blinks, movement, electrode pops) can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD. Taking the median across Welch segments instead is a robust estimator that keeps the spectrum of the clean resting background. This should help the relative band-power markers of schizophrenia (more delta/theta, less alpha), and it should hold up better on the external clinics' data.

Schizophrenia is linked to a slower alpha rhythm and more power in the upper theta and lower alpha range. The 5 broad bands blur that shift, so I'm splitting theta, alpha and beta into sub-bands (theta 4–6/6–8, alpha 8–10/10–13, beta 13–20/20–30). This lets the linear model pick up where power sits inside each band while staying on relative power, which doesn't depend on amplitude scale.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few movement, EMG or electrode-pop segments can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD and hide the spectral differences in schizophrenia (more slow-wave power, less alpha). The only change is to average the Welch segments by median instead of mean. Median averaging resists artifacts, and its constant bias cancels out in relative band power. It should also hold up better on the external sets from other clinics. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.
